title: Git Flow (branching strategies)
objectives: Understand branching strategies via a real-life analogy
Distinguish Git Flow, GitHub Flow, GitLab Flow, Trunk-Based
Pick a strategy per team size + release cadence
Handle hot-fixes, release branches, and long-lived branches
Manage feature flags with trunk-based development

sections.markdown:
**Think of branching strategies as different orchestral scores for the same instruments.**

Every team has git branches; how they're structured determines the collaboration rhythm.

- **Git Flow (Vincent Driessen, 2010)** — classical + heavy: `main`, `develop`, `feature/*`, `release/*`, `hotfix/*`. Great for scheduled releases (mobile apps historically); slow when you deploy daily.
- **GitHub Flow** — minimalist: `main` + short-lived feature branches; deploy from main. Great for web apps that ship continuously.
- **GitLab Flow** — GitHub Flow + environment branches (`main` → `staging` → `production`).
- **Trunk-based (Google-style)** — everyone commits to main; features hidden behind flags; deploys many times a day. Requires strong test discipline.

**Why picking the right strategy matters for Flutter apps:** mobile has store-approval delays (Play + App Store take hours), which biases toward release-branch strategies. But heavy strategies (Git Flow's `develop` branch) create merge headaches. Modern Flutter teams often use **simplified GitHub Flow with release branches**: main is always releasable, release branches cut on schedule, hotfixes cherry-picked.

**Branching strategy** = the team's conventions for how branches map to work-in-progress, releases, and environments. Popular models: **Git Flow** (main + develop + release + hotfix + feature; scheduled releases), **GitHub Flow** (main + short feature branches; continuous deploy), **GitLab Flow** (adds environment branches), **Trunk-Based Development** (single main + short-lived branches or direct commits; feature flags gate incomplete work). Choice driven by release cadence + team size + risk tolerance.

sections.markdown: ## Modern mobile branching (recommended default)
## Common mistakes
**Mistake 1: Long-lived feature branches.** Rebased daily onto main = merge hell + drift; ship earlier + flag it.
**Mistake 2: `develop` branch (Git Flow) without release discipline.** Becomes a mirror of main + no benefit.
**Mistake 3: Direct commits to main.** Skips PR review + CI checks.
**Mistake 4: Skipping hotfix branches.** Fixing on main + shipping directly = risky.
**Mistake 5: Hotfix not backported to main.** Same bug reappears in next release.
**Mistake 6: No branch protection rules.** Anyone can force-push to main.
**Mistake 7: Trunk-based without feature flags.** Incomplete work in main = broken UI in prod.
**Mistake 8: Copy-paste Git Flow with no team need.** Overhead > benefit for small teams.
## Best practices
**1. Pick the simplest strategy that fits your cadence.**
**2. Main always releasable** (green + shippable).
**3. Short-lived feature branches** (< 3 days).
**4. Branch protection rules** — required reviews + green CI + linear history.
**5. Feature flags for incomplete work** — Remote Config / launch darkly.
**6. Release branches** for store cadence.
**7. Hotfix branch + backport to main.**
**8. Tag every release** with semver.
## Practice programs
**Practice 1 (Easy)** — GitHub Flow: feature branch + PR + merge.
**Practice 2 (Medium)** — Release branch cut + hotfix + backport.
**Practice 3 (Medium)** — Branch protection rules on main.
**Practice 4 (Hard)** — Trunk-based dev with Remote Config feature flag.
**Practice 5 (Expert)** — Migrate a Git Flow repo to release-branch model + document.
## Interview Q&A

**Q1: Git Flow vs GitHub Flow — pick when?**

**A:** **Git Flow** was designed for scheduled releases with multiple parallel versions in production (banks maintaining 3 concurrent app versions). The `develop` + `release` + `hotfix` branches provide isolation. **Cost:** heavyweight; merging back-and-forth generates conflicts; onboarding slow. **GitHub Flow** — `main` + short feature branches; deploy from main. Optimized for continuous-deployment web apps. **For Flutter apps in 2026:** most teams use a hybrid — `main` + feature branches (GitHub Flow) + release branches for store submissions (small piece of Git Flow). Pure Git Flow is overkill for most modern teams; pure GitHub Flow doesn't fit store-approval delays. **Interview signal:** knowing the trade-offs + not being dogmatic.

**Q2: What is trunk-based development + when does it work?**

**A:** **Trunk-based** = everyone commits to `main` (the trunk) directly or via very short-lived branches; deploys happen from main many times a day. **Requires:** (1) fast automated tests (< 10 min from commit to green build); (2) strong CI (blocks broken builds); (3) feature flags to hide incomplete work; (4) code review discipline (PRs merged within hours). **Wins when:** high-velocity teams (Google, Meta, Netflix), continuous deployment web/backend, tight test coverage. **Fails when:** slow CI, weak tests, no feature-flag infrastructure. **Mobile challenge:** store-approval delays make 'many deploys a day' impossible; but you can still trunk-develop + batch releases from main. **Interviewer signal:** understanding the DISCIPLINE it requires + why some teams don't do it.

**Q3: How do you handle a hot-fix mid-release?**

**A:** **Scenario:** v1.2.0 is in production; a critical bug is reported. Main has moved on to v1.3.0 features. **Steps:** (1) **Branch from the release tag** — `git switch -c hotfix/1.2.1 v1.2.0`. (2) **Fix + commit** — minimal, targeted change; add a regression test. (3) **CI on hotfix branch** — full suite must pass. (4) **PR + review** — expedited but still reviewed. (5) **Tag** `v1.2.1` + build store artifacts + submit. (6) **Backport to main** — `git switch main; git cherry-pick <hotfix-sha>` OR merge the hotfix branch into main. (7) **Also backport to any other active release branches.** (8) **Post-mortem** — how did the bug escape tests? add coverage. **Regulator/pharma apps:** hotfix may skip normal review due to safety. **Interviewer signal:** knowing hotfixes are branched FROM the release tag, not from main.

**Q4: What role do feature flags play in branching strategies?**

**A:** **Feature flags decouple deployment from release.** Code lands in main + is deployed but hidden behind a flag; UI only enables when flag flips (Remote Config, LaunchDarkly). **Enables:** (1) **Trunk-based development** — incomplete work merges + hides. (2) **Gradual rollouts** — 1% → 10% → 100%. (3) **Kill switches** — instant off for a bad feature without redeploy. (4) **A/B tests** — variant A + variant B in the same build. (5) **Environment differences** — dev sees experimental features, prod doesn't. **Cost:** flag debt — old flags left in code become tangled; sunset flags after 100% rollout. **In Flutter mobile:** Firebase Remote Config is the common infrastructure; LaunchDarkly for enterprise. **Interviewer signal:** understanding branching + flagging as complementary tools.

**Q5: How would you set up branch protection rules on GitHub?**

**A:** On `main` (and release branches): **(1) Require pull request** before merging. **(2) Require approvals** — 1-2 reviewers minimum. **(3) Require status checks to pass** — CI (build + test + lint) + code coverage threshold + security scan. **(4) Require branches up to date** — merge only if the PR is rebased/merged with latest main. **(5) Require signed commits** — GPG/SSH signatures (SOC 2). **(6) Require linear history** — no merge commits (forces squash-merge or rebase-merge). **(7) Restrict who can push** — bots + release automation only for main. **(8) Restrict force pushes + deletions.** **(9) Require conversation resolution** — all PR comments addressed. **(10) Include administrators** — even the CEO follows the rules. **(11) CODEOWNERS** — auto-request reviews from domain experts. Interviewer signal: comprehensive setup + rationale.

**Q6: How do you handle branching in a monorepo?**

**A:** **Monorepo challenges:** thousands of PRs touching different packages; slow CI unless you skip unaffected tests. **Strategies:** (1) **Path-based CI filters** — GitHub Actions `paths:` filter runs only jobs affected by changed files. (2) **Bazel / Nx / Turborepo** — compute affected packages and their downstream deps. (3) **Trunk-based** — long-lived branches are impossible; small commits + fast merge. (4) **Melos (Flutter)** — coordinated versioning across packages. (5) **CODEOWNERS by directory** — right reviewers auto-assigned. (6) **PR templates** — 'which package(s) changed?' checkbox. (7) **Merge queue** — batches PRs to avoid main-conflict rebases. **Google's monorepo (Piper)** uses trunk-based + massive CI + strict code review + very few branches — the extreme example. **Interviewer bonus:** knowing monorepos favor trunk-based.

## Real-world usage

- **Small-to-mid Flutter apps** — GitHub Flow + release branches.
- **Enterprise banking apps** — modified Git Flow with parallel versions.
- **Startups** — trunk-based with feature flags.
- **Monorepos** — trunk-based + Melos/Nx.

## Advanced notes

- **Merge queue (GitHub)** — batches + serializes PR merges; avoids race conditions.
- **Semantic-release** — automated version bump + changelog based on commit messages.
- **`main` vs `master`** — GitHub defaults to `main` since 2020.
- **Release cadence signals** — daily = trunk-based; weekly = GitHub Flow + release branches; monthly = release branches or Git Flow.
- **Long-lived feature flags** = tech debt; sunset ceremony.
- **Melos + monorepo Flutter** — coordinated pubspec versioning.
- **Hotfix from production tag** — always branch from the exact deployed sha.
- **Auto-merge** — PR merges when checks pass; useful for dependency-bump PRs.
- **Draft PRs** — early feedback without CI cost.
- **CODEOWNERS** — required reviewers per directory.
- **`Renovate` / `Dependabot`** — auto-PRs for dependency updates.
